Histology shows well‑circumscribed, homogeneous eosinophilic, fissured (clefted) deposits in the subepithelial connective tissue beneath an atrophic epithelium, with scarce fibroblasts. Crucial special stain results: Congo red negative (rules against true amyloid) and Verhoeff–van Gieson / Orcein demonstrating fragmented elastic fibers at the periphery and within the colloid material. The combination of amorphous eosinophilic material with clefts, absence of Congo red positivity, and demonstration of altered/fragmented elastic fibers is most consistent with a colloid/elastotic degeneration process (colloid milium–type change) rather than true amyloid or a cellular tumor. Colloid milium (colloid degeneration) classically shows homogeneous eosinophilic colloid in the dermis with clefting and association with elastic fiber degeneration; although the cutaneous form typically affects sun‑exposed skin, rare mucosal (oral) colloid degeneration/colloid deposits of the tongue have been described and fit the clinical–pathologic picture here. Other possibilities that can appear as yellowish tongue papules or plaques and must be considered include nodular (localized) amyloidosis (clinically similar but excluded by Congo red negativity), ectopic sebaceous glands (Fordyce spots), granular cell tumor (common on the tongue and can be yellowish), and verrucous (verruciform) squamous lesions (including verrucous carcinoma) given the cobblestone morphology.

DIAGNOSIS:
1. Mucosal colloid degeneration / colloid milium–type (colloid deposits of the tongue; elastotic/colloid degeneration of oral mucosa) – most likely
2. Localized (nodular) oral amyloidosis – less likely (clinically similar but ruled out by negative Congo red)
3. Fordyce spots (ectopic sebaceous glands of oral mucosa) – possible clinically (yellow papules) but histology does not match
4. Granular cell tumor (Abrikossoff tumor) of the tongue – consideration for solitary/yellowish tongue nodules, but histology would show granular S‑100+ cells rather than amorphous eosinophilic colloid
5. Verrucous squamous lesion / verrucous carcinoma or reactive verruciform hyperplasia – included because of cobblestone/verrucous appearance, but histology lacks epithelial dysplasia/invasion so this is less likely
